name: California
title: Tax the rich — sometimes. California voters sent mixed signals with ballot measures
description: California voters shot down a tax on billionaires' assets but said yes to a high-income tax. They were just two of the five tax questions on the ballot.
text:
In summary
California voters shot down a tax on billionaires’ assets but said yes to a high-income tax. They were just two of the five tax questions on the ballot.


California voters faced big questions about money in this election, and the results sent mixed signals about how the electorate feels about taxation.
They want to tax the rich — but only sometimes. They want the money counters at the Franchise Tax Board to stay far away from personal assets, but are leaving the door open for future taxes or taxes on other people.
On Election Day, voters: 

Rejected Proposition 40, an effort to levy a first-of-its-kind wealth tax on billionaires
Rejected Proposition 41, a taxation transparency measure 
Approved Proposition 42, a ban on wealth taxes and retroactive taxes 
Rejected Proposition 43, an attempt to make it more difficult for local governments to raise taxes
Approved Proposition 3, a proposal to make permanent a tax on high-income earners

Voters also approved several high-profile local taxes, including two measures to fund the Bay Area’s regional transit systems, including Muni and BART, and a half-cent sales tax to fund firefighting in the city of Los Angeles.
The mixed outcome, experts say, shows that California voters are embracing tax hikes — but only when they can ensure the money is funding tangible services they support.
“Voters are willing to open up their wallet if they believe it’s for a good cause … and that it’s actually going to that place,” said Brandon Castillo, a prominent ballot measure strategist in California.
It also demonstrates voters’ willingness to support taxes that likely won’t affect their own pocketbook, said Mark Baldassare, survey director of the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California.
“We are a very progressive state where voters, particularly today when affordability weighs on them, have a tendency to say somebody else will be paying taxes, not me.”
Still, that “not me” attitude didn’t stretch as far as the state’s contentious billionaire tax, which faced opposition from business interests, Democrats and deep-pocketed Silicon Valley executives alike.
Why did the billionaire tax fail?
The failure of the billionaire tax represents the most stunning defeat of Election Day for progressive Democrats who tried unsuccessfully to capitalize on souring sentiment toward the ultra-wealthy amid high gas prices and worsening inflation for average Californians. How could the most progressive measure in the most progressive state fail during a “blue wave” election?
“California voters are sometimes more conservative on ballot propositions than they are on voting for candidates,” said Christian Grose, a political science and public policy professor at USC.
In recent years, voters through ballot measures got tougher on crime, shot down a minimum wage increase and rejected efforts to make it easier to pass local bonds. In fact, voters upheld the death penalty the last time it appeared on the ballot even though the state has not executed anyone since 2006. In a historic decision, Gov. Gavin Newsom also earlier this month commuted all death row sentences to life without parole. 
Rob Stutzman, a Republican political consultant, said this trend likely holds true because ballot initiatives — including taxation questions — generally ask voters to consider one issue at a time and are presented in a nonpartisan manner. In contrast, voting for a liberal or conservative candidate requires voters to weigh multiple aspects of a person’s record, character or values.
“They just have the policy question, and voters sort it out for themselves,” Stutzman said.
Those centrist tendencies helped push Prop. 42, one of two measures put on the ballot by billionaires trying to protect their wealth, across the finish line. That measure bans taxes on personal property, business interests and financial investments. The Associated Press confirmed its passage by 51.3% Friday.
Anti-tax and union supporters touted it as a way to protect retirement savings and pensions potentially targeted by the billionaire tax, though billionaire tax proponents countered that their measure never targeted ordinary retirement accounts in the first place.
Experts say voter confusion and a $378 million opposition warchest donated primarily by Silicon Valley tech billionaires doomed the billionaire tax.
Props. 41 and 42 were designed specifically to kill Prop. 40 if it had passed, creating a chaotic array of choices. The billionaire tax also amassed a coalition of diverse and vocal opponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, Planned Parenthood, medical clinics and the state’s largest teachers union, despite the California Democratic Party and California Labor Federation supporting it.
Polling showed support for the measure dropped 6 points in the last two months before the election, taking it from a narrow lead to a crushing defeat. 
“The campaign against the billionaire tax was a success,” Grose said.
Other taxes succeeded
But few view the results on Prop. 40 as a referendum on the state’s progressive tax system. Instead, many analysts said it was simply bad policy that splintered California’s Democratic base.
Prop. 40 aimed to focus almost all the revenue in healthcare while cutting out other areas of state spending, which would lose funding if billionaires left the state and stopped paying income taxes, said Thad Kousser, a political science professor at UC San Diego. That, he said, was “an unforced error.” 
“It made it a David and Goliath fight, but it didn’t need to be,” he said. “You don’t pass a landmark progressive tax increase that is sort of a change to how America has historically done anything by dividing up the progressive coalition.”
At the same time, Prop. 42’s anti-taxation sentiment was also somewhat tempered by the defeat of Prop. 43, which would have made increasing taxes for local public services more difficult, and the success of Prop. 3, which sticks a higher tax bracket on high-income earners to help fund schools.
Prop. 43 would have required a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax dedicated to specific services. Kousser said voters are concerned the measure would allow for “minority rule,” where just a third of voters would be able to block essential funding for local services.
“Voters don’t like to put in place these rules that seem to be tilted in one direction,” he said.
David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, said Prop. 3’s passage sent a “resounding message of support for taxing the wealthy.” That measure passed with nearly 59% of the vote and sets a higher tax bracket on individually earned income above $360,000.
People in that income bracket have been paying that extra tax since 2012 as a temporary state budget fix; Prop. 3 made it permanent.
Why could voters distinguish between the income tax Prop. 3 and the wealth tax in Prop. 40? Partly because Prop. 3 had no opposition among Democrats, Kousser noted. It also extended an existing tax, whereas Prop. 40 opponents ran ads claiming that state lawmakers could come after average Californians’ personal savings.
Ballot box tempting for revenue seekers
Dustin Corcoran, chief executive of the California Medical Association, which opposed the billionaire tax, said he also does not view its defeat “as an endorsement of wealth inequality or the status quo.”
The state still needs to find a way to securely finance healthcare, education and other core services, Corcoran said, and the medical association is exploring future ballot initiative options to generate revenue. 
Not even Prop. 40’s supporters view its defeat as a reason to stop trying to tax the ultra-wealthy in California. Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponents of the billionaire tax, vowed to come back in 2028 with another billionaire tax initiative.
Regan also pushed back on the notion that Democrats were divided on wealth taxes, arguing that polling showed between 60% to 70% of Democrats supported the measure and only Democratic leaders such as Newsom and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra opposed it. 
“At the very highest levels of state officials there’s actually, you know, a different point of view, but that’s out of step with where regular people are at,” Regan said. 
Still, fiscal conservatives, the state’s non-partisan budget analyst, and even some moderate Democrats say taxation cannot be the only solution to California’s budget woes. The state has faced four consecutive deficit years and spending that outpaces revenue despite the budget as a whole growing. The current state budget calls for $351.7 billion in total spending — a 64% increase over the $214.8 billion Newsom signed in his first year as governor seven years ago.
“California’s budget is structurally overextended despite booming and near-record revenues,” the Legislative Analyst’s Office wrote in a new budget assessment. “This overextended budget reflects a higher ongoing spending base; diminished reserves; an already accumulated wall of debt; and annual, out-year operating deficits of $8 billion to $10 billion.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Commentary: Wisconsin Democrats have their work cut out for them
description: There are a lot of big things Democrats in Wisconsin can do with their new, trifecta control of state government. text:
Scaffolding on the State Capitol of Wisconsin | Photo by Greg AndersonThere are a lot of big things Democrats in Wisconsin can do with their new, trifecta control of state government. Reinvesting in public schools — and shifting the burden for keeping schools afloat off local property taxpayers — would be a great start. So would overturning Act 10 (unless the state Supreme Court beats them to it), restoring the prevailing wage law and getting rid of so-called right-to-work legislation, thus reversing the largest decline in union representation in any state over the last 40 years. Add to that getting rid of PFAS, preserving public land, creating a nonpartisan redistricting process that ends gerrymandering once and for all. All of these things are possible when the new governor and Legislature get to work. 
While state officials can’t reverse federal policies that are driving up the cost of living, let alone end the disastrous Iran war, they can do a lot to improve the material wellbeing of state residents just by turning the page on 15 years of austerity.
Wisconsin is sitting on a state budget surplus that mostly represents the money the state no longer pays to support schools. For more than a decade, Wisconsin has let its education historic system degrade while hoarding that money. 
At the same time, local property taxpayers are overextended and grouchy from years of reaching into their own pockets to make up for the state’s failure to support schools.
Former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker’s assault on unions hurt teachers and other public employees directly, but it also created a much harsher, leaner environment for working people across Wisconsin and their families. 
A recent report by the Illinois Economic Policy Institute highlights the ways anti-union policies in Wisconsin have harmed the middle class, degraded a once-great public school system and made life more expensive and less secure for working families. 
This was not what Walker and his allies advertised when they pioneered the divide-and-conquer politics that pushed down union membership, wages and labor force participation for both union and non-union workers. 
Supposedly, busting teachers’ unions was going to give schools the budget flexibility to do more with less, and slashing state funding for education would mean lower taxes. Instead, schools went into a long financial slide, accompanied by cuts to programs, increasing class sizes and declining test scores, while property tax rates soared. 
Walker and the Republicans talked a lot about making Wisconsin “open for business” and ushering in a new era of prosperity. But the promised 250,000 new private sector jobs never materialized, and wages, job growth and GDP languished compared to our neighboring Great Lakes states, as “data wonk” Bruce Thompson wrote in an analysis for Urban Milwaukee of the effects of Act 10.
All of this, plus Republicans’ stubborn refusal to accept the federal Medicaid expansion for years before President Donald Trump’s massive assault on healthcare, contributed to Wisconsinites’ particular struggles with affordability — the issue that drove the blue tsunami across the country in the 2026 midterms.
Voters in the last election expressed serious doubt about some of the core tenets of Republican economic policy, including the idea that tax breaks for the very rich will make us all more prosperous, and spending on schools and other basic social goods is a burdensome waste. 
In the Republican radio address this week, incoming Republican Senate minority leader Julian Bradley acknowledged the stunning midterm rebuke to his party, saying “folks who are struggling to get by want to know that there’s a path to get ahead.”
“We hear you,” he said on behalf of his fellow members of Wisconsin’s severely diminished Republican caucus. Then he doubled down on the philosophy that got them where they are today: “If the new Democrat majority wants to focus on affordability, then we should be talking about meaningful tax cuts, returning the surplus to the families who earned it and clearing away the red tape that makes it harder to build a home or hire a worker.”
If voters wanted more of the same Republican tax cuts and deregulation Bradley is pushing, and which reached a new peak with Trump’s massive “One Big Beautiful” transfer of wealth from the many to the few, the election wouldn’t have gone the way it did.
According to Bradley, Democrats are talking about “higher taxes, more spending, redrawing maps” and “not a single one of these ideas will lower your grocery bills.”
It’s true that ending Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran that is driving record-high diesel prices would be the fastest route to cheaper groceries. But state Democrats can do a lot to improve Wisconsinites’ economic wellbeing by bringing back middle class jobs and union protections that raise wages. Using state money to support schools will lower property taxes. Investing in healthcare, child care, mass transit, environmental protection and clean energy will improve the economy and the future of our state.
Wisconsinites are eager to see government get to work to get those things done.

Ma hope o ka ‘elua me ka hapa pule ma hope o ka loku ‘ino ‘ana o ka ua i ka ‘Ino Lala a he kiliona a ʻoi kālani ua e waiho maila mai ʻō a ʻō o ka pae ʻāina, hoʻopuka akula ko Honolulu he kūkala nūhou nona kahi helu e hopohopo ʻia: Ua hanini ma kahi o ka 26 miliona kālani kūkae nona ke koʻohune ma ke Awa O Honolulu i ka ʻino nui.
ʻO ia paha kekahi o nā hanini keu a ka maikaʻi ʻole mai ka makahiki 2006 mai, i ka wā i hanini ai ʻaneʻane he 50 miliona kālani kūkae i loko o ke Alawai Ala Wai he hopena o ka ua nui.

“He kākaʻikahi kēia,” i ʻōlelo ai ʻo Roger Babcock, ka Luna Hoʻokele o ke Keʻena Lawelawe ‘Āina o Honolulu, ma kahi nīnauele hope iho nei.
I ke kūlanakauhale e ʻimi ana i ka hoʻolilo i ke kālā ma nā biliona ma luna o nā hoʻokāʻoi ʻauwai i koi ʻia na ke aupuni pekelala, aia ke ʻaʻa ʻia nei ka ikaika o ia mau hoʻokāʻoi ʻana e nā ʻino e like me Lala, a ke hoʻokikina ʻia nei nā ʻelele hoʻokō e lapaʻau i nā pilikia hou i wānana mua ʻole ʻia.
ʻO ka hapa nui o ka hanini ʻana — he 26.1 miliona kālani kona nui — ʻo ke keʻakeʻa o nā kānana i ka ʻōpala ma ka Hale Hoʻomaʻemaʻe Wai Kūkae o Sand Island ka mole o ka pilikia, wahi a ke kūkala nūhou, a kaumaha iho ai ka wai kūkae a komo ihola i nā ʻauwai hoʻokuʻu wai ʻino.
Aia ke hoʻokāʻoi nui loa ʻia nei ka Hale Hoʻomaʻemaʻe Wai Kūkae o Sand Island i mea e hahai ai i nā lula maʻemaʻe kūkae pekelala. David Croxford/Civil Beat/2025
ʻO ka hanini ʻana o ka 26 miliona kālani kūkae o ʻAukake kekahi o nā mea nui loa ma ka hoʻomanaʻo ʻana aʻe iho nei.
ʻO ka hanini ʻana o ke 50 miliona kālani kūkae i ka makahiki 2005, ua hanini hoʻi ma kahi wā kaulana i ka loku nui o ka ua no ke 40 lā moekahi, a pani ʻia ai nā kahakai mai Magic Island i Fort DeRussy.
Mau ka hiki ke pā ka poʻe a mea like paha i ke kūkae ma kona ʻano ʻuʻuku. I ka makahiki 2015, he kumu ka ʻIno Kilo i hanini ai ʻaneʻane he hapa miliona kālani kūkae ma kahi kokoke i ka huina alanui Atkinson a me Ala Moana, a pani ʻia ai nā ala kai mai ke Kahakai ʻo Kūhiō a i Kakaʻako.
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Babcock, ʻaʻole i keʻakeʻa nā kānana ma nā wā ʻē aʻe i loku ai ka ua a ʻaʻole i wānana ʻia ka lilo ʻana o ia mea he pilikia ma lalo o ka ʻaelike pekelala e hoʻokele nei i ka hoʻokāʻoi ʻia o ko Honolulu ʻōnaehana hoʻokuʻu wai kūkae. ʻAʻole nō hoʻi i keʻakeʻa nā kānana i nā ʻino Kona moekahi o Malaki, wahi āna, a no laila, he paʻakikī ka ʻike ponoʻī i ka papahana e lawelawe ai i mea e loaʻa ʻole ai kēia ʻano i ka wā e hiki mai ana. Ke hai nei ke kūlanakauhale he kanaka ʻike e noiʻi ai i ka pilikia.
“He mea nui ko mākou kālailai pono ʻana i kēia,” wahi a Babcock i ʻōlelo ai.
‘Ma Hea Kākou E Hoʻokahe Ai?’
I ka wā a kekahi e hoʻoholo ai he lua ma kahi kūlanakauhale ʻo Honolulu, holo ia wai i loko o kekahi mau paipu e holo ana i ka Hale Hoʻomaʻemaʻe Wai Kūkae o Sand Island, kahi e hoʻomaʻemaʻe ʻia ai ma kahi o ke 60 miliona kālani wai kūkae i kēlā me kēia lā ma mua o ka hoʻokuʻu ʻia i loko o ke kai. Hiki nō naʻe ke kupu mai nā pilikia.
Lawelawe ʻia ke kūkae ma nā paipu ma o nā ʻano pauma uila a ʻumekaumaha. Inā kahiko loa nā paipu, hiki ke haki, a hanini ai ka wai kūkae. A inā pau ka pono o kahi pauma — ma muli paha o ka pio o ka uila a no ka pilikia o kahi hoʻopaʻa — hiki ke ulu ke kaumaha o ka wai kūkae, a hanini ai paha. I mea e hoʻomaʻemaʻe ʻia ai ia hanini ʻana, kiʻi ke kūlanakauhale i nā kalaka wākiuma.
Ua pilikia mua ke kūlanakauhale ma ke kānāwai i nā hanini wai kūkae pinepine. I mea e hoʻopau ʻia ai kahi mau hihia kānāwai no nā hanini mai nā hui e like ma ka Sierra Club, ua komo ko Honolulu i kahi kūkala ʻae poepoe honua me ke aupuni pekelala i ka makahiki 2010 nona kekahi mau hana: ʻO ka hoʻoikaika i kona ʻōnaehana paipu a me ke ke kiʻi i kahi kiʻina hoʻomaʻemaʻe wai nōhihi aʻe ma kona mau hale hoʻomaʻemaʻe wai kūkae.
“Ma ka laulā, ʻo ke ola kino o ke ākea ka hopohopo nui,” wahi a Babcock. “Ua hoʻonoho ʻia nā lula a mea like i mea e kaupalena ai i ka pā o ke ākea i ka wai kūkae.”
Ua holo ka ʻāpana hana mua a ke kūlanakauhale ma lalo o ke kūkala — ʻo ka hoʻokāʻoi i kekahi mau paipu he kenekulia kona kahiko i mea e hoʻēmi ʻia ai nā hanini ʻana ma nā alanui kūlanakauhale — mai ka makahiki 2010 i ka makahiki 2020.
A laila, i mea e hoʻoheheʻe ʻia ai ke kūkae paʻa, ua kauoha ʻia ma lalo o ke kūkala ka hoʻokomo ʻana he lawelawe huna ola — he ʻōnaehana no ka hoʻoheheʻe ʻana i ke kūkae a me ka wehe ʻana i nā mea kūpono ʻole ma kahi o ka hoʻokaʻawale wale ʻana aku nō i ke kūkae paʻa mai ka wai kūkae — i nā Hale Hoʻomaʻemaʻe Wai Kūkae o Sand Island a me Honouliuli. Ua pau ka hana ma Honouliuli ma ka makahiki 2024, a ua kō iho nei ke keʻehina mua o kēia hana ma Sand Island i kēlā mahina aku nei me ka palena pau loa i ka makahiki 2035.
Ma mua o ka hoʻokuʻu ʻana i ka wai kūkae i hoʻomaʻemaʻe ʻia i ke kai, hoʻokaʻawale ko ka Hale Hoʻomaʻemaʻe Wai Kūkae o Sand Island i ke kūkae paʻa mai ka wai kūkae me ka ʻumekaumaha ma nā kiʻo wai poepoe nui, a i ʻole paha ia, he kānana. Ke koi nei ke aupuni pekelala e hoʻokomo ko Sand Island he lawelawe huna ola kekahi. David Croxford/Civil Beat/2025
Hōʻike ʻia ma ka ʻikepili kūlanakauhale ke emi ʻana o ka nui hanini ʻana mai ka 200 i ke 31 ma waena o nā makahiki 2006 i ka 2024.
            Ma ka wā o nā ʻino nui, wahi a Babcock, hoʻāʻo kāna mau limahana e hoʻoholo i ka wai kūkae i nā hale hoʻomaʻemaʻe wai kūkae i mea e hōʻalo ʻia ai ka hanini ʻana o ka wai kūkae ma nā alanui.
“ʻAʻole paha hiki ke ʻalo ʻia ka hanini ʻana o ka wai kūkae i kekahi manawa,” wahi āna. “No laila, e pono mākou ma ke ʻano he keʻena e hoʻoholo: Ma hea ana kākou e hoʻokahe ai?” 
Aia ma ka Hale Hoʻomaʻemaʻe Wai Kūkae o Sand Island ka hapa nui loa o ka hanini ʻana o ka wai kūkae ma ka wā o Lala. Ua hiki ke loaʻa hou mai i ke kūlanakauhale he hapa miliona a ʻoi kālani o ka wai kūkae i hanini mai Sand Island, e waiho ana nō naʻe he 25.45 miliona kālani wai kūkae i hanini i loko o nā ʻauwai hoʻokuʻu wai e holo ana i ke Awa o Honolulu. Ua hiki i nā limahana ke lapaʻau i ka pilikia ma ke kālele ma luna o ka hoʻomaʻemaʻe i ka ʻōpala mai kekahi kānana, he mea hoʻi i maha iho ai ke kaumaha o nā kānana ʻē aʻe a ʻekolu i pilikia, a pēlā i hiki ai i nā limahana ke hoʻomaʻemaʻe i ia mau mea.
Aia ma Kakaʻako ma Kahi Pauma Wai Kūkae o Ala Moana nā hanini ʻē aʻe o ia lā ma muli o ka pio ʻana o ka uila a me ka pilikia o kahi hoʻopaʻa ma kahi mīkini uila keu, kahi i hanini ai he 700,000 kālani wai kūkae a i loaʻa hou mai ai he 150,000 kālani wai kūkae. Ua kaumaha pū ka wai kūkae ma kahi kokoke ma 425 South Alanui i ia mau pio ʻana o ka uila, kahi i hoʻokahe ai nā manakia hale i ka wai kūkae ma Auahi Alanui e mālama ʻia ai ko ka hale ʻōnaehana uila, wahi a ke kūkala nūhou kūlanakauhale.
Ua lawe ʻia mai kēia kūkae paʻa i kahi hale hoʻoulu meakanu ma ke ʻano he kīpulu pōkā. David Croxford/Civil Beat/2025
Eia hou, ua hālana kahi ʻīpuka ʻauwai ma kahi kokoke i kahi o hope loa o ke Awāwa ʻo Mānoa, a hanini ai he 100 miliona kālani wai kūkae. Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Babcock, he pilikia pinepine ia wahi a hoʻonoho ʻo ia i nā limahana ma laila me nā kalaka wākiuma ma nā wā ʻino a hiki i ka wā e hik ai i kona keʻena ke hoʻoponopono pau loa i ia pilikia ma laila.
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Steve Holmes, he lālā o ka ʻaha kalana o ke kūlanakauhale ʻo Honolulu ma mua a ʻo ka lālā hoʻokaʻaʻike o ka Sierra Club e makaʻala ana i ka holomua o ke kūlanakauhale no ke kūkala, ʻo ka ʻoiaʻiʻo, he kaʻawale ko Honolulu mau ʻōnaehana kiʻo wai ua a kiʻo wai kūkae. Kulu nō naʻe ka wai ua i nā māwae o ka ʻōnaehana wai kūkae, wahi āna, a kaumaha hou ai ka ʻōnaehana hoʻomaʻemaʻe wai kūkae ke nui loa ka wai kahe.
“ʻIke au, ʻaʻole hauʻoli ka poʻe i ka piʻi ʻana o ka uku ʻauwai,” wahi a Holmes, e kuhikuhi ana i ka piʻi ʻana aku nei o ka uku no ka uku ʻana i nā hoʻokāʻoi ʻana, “akā, ma ko mākou hoʻomaka mua ʻana i kēia hana, aia iā mākou nā ʻōnaehana paipu he 100 makahiki kona kahiko ma Honolulu. A ua pilikia loa ihola kona kūlana.”

name: VTDigger
title: Chittenden parents file lawsuit challenging Vermont’s new public tuition rules
description:
A family is suing the state in federal court, arguing that Vermont’s 2025 education reform law is unconstitutional because it excludes religious schools from receiving public tuition dollars. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Chittenden parents file lawsuit challenging Vermont’s new public tuition rules.
text:
Champlain Valley School District school busses in Hinesburg in Jan. 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Two Chittenden parents are suing the Vermont Agency of Education in federal court, alleging Vermont illegally excludes religious schools from being eligible for the state’s public tuition program for private schools. 
The lawsuit, filed by Carrie and Greg Bishop, alleges that the requirements for private schools to receive public tuition dollars under Vermont’s 2025 education reform law “create a de facto religious exclusion” that violates the First Amendment. 
“They’re not receiving equal treatment, yet they deserve equal access to public funding alongside other families in the state,” said Jacob Reed, the lawyer representing the Bishop family, in an interview. Reed works for Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative Christian legal organization based in Arizona that is increasingly involved in state politics and has previously challenged the constitutionality of Vermont’s public tuition program.  
The Bishop family alleges they’re experiencing religious discrimination. And their lawsuit isn’t the first of its kind. 
Toren Ballard, a spokesperson for the state Agency of Education, declined to comment on the ongoing case. The Vermont Attorney General’s Office is representing the agency in the suit, he said. 
Some rural school districts in Vermont lack public schools for all grades. Through the state’s public tuition system, families can send their kids to private schools or public schools in another district on the public dime. About 3,500 kids in Vermont received public tuition as of 2024, according to the education agency. 
Private religious schools were formerly included in the program and saw an influx of public dollars in recent years. But that practice ended in 2025 when the state passed a wide ranging education reform law, Act 73, that created new qualifications for private schools to be included in the tuition program. 
To qualify under the new law, a school had to be in a district that doesn’t operate a public school for some or all grade levels and at least 25% of their student body from the 2023-24 school year had to be funded by a Vermont public school district. 
After the passage of Act 73, only 18 private schools — none of which is religious — qualified for the public tuition program.
While Act 73 eliminated all religious schools from the tuition program, it eliminated an even larger number of secular schools, according to court documents from a previous lawsuit challenging the law. Eighteen secular schools were eliminated from the program, while 15 Catholic and Christian schools were eliminated. 
“The idea is to have, frankly, as many Vermont kids under the roof of Vermont’s public schools as possible, in order to have that scale and reduce our-per pupil costs,” said Rep. Peter Conlon, D-Cornwall, who chairs the House Education Committee and helped craft Act 73. 
The tuition program exists, Conlon said, because lawmakers recognize that public schools aren’t easily accessible in some parts of the state. 
But Reed sees things differently. 
“What is happening here is people of faith are essentially being treated as second-class citizens,” said Reed, who specializes in representing Christian ministries and religious schools in First Amendment cases.

READ MORE

Courts in Vermont  and around the country have long grappled with the legality of excluding religious schools from receiving public tuition. 
The U.S. Supreme Court issued a landmark 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, ruling that Maine’s public tuition program, which is similar to Vermont’s, couldn’t deny funds to some parents based on how they exercise their religion. The decision reverberated through Vermont and opened up more public tuition funds for religious schools — until the 2025 law went into effect. 
Alliance Defending Freedom has filed at least five lawsuits challenging Vermont’s public tuition system, although not all of them address the state’s 2025 law, according to Reed. The firm also represented the Mid Vermont Christian School, which sued the state in 2023 after it was banned from participating in state athletics because it forfeited against a team with a transgender player. 
A federal appeals court ruled in the school’s favor in September 2025 and said its teams must be allowed to participate, but returned the case to the lower court for further action. Last year the school also filed a new legal lawsuit challenging Act 73. A decision in the case is still pending, Reed said. 
The Bishops’ legal challenge explains why they allege religious discrimination. 
“Public schools teach evolution, which conflicts with the Bishops’ religious teachings that God created the universe in seven days,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit also said that the Bishops’ older sons “faced backlash and scrutiny” for bringing their bibles to public school with them. 
The family lives in the Barstow Unified Union School District, which only has public schools through eighth grade. Rather than sending their daughters to public schools through the tuition program like they did with their sons, the couple wanted to send their daughters to a religious school. 
The couple decided to send their daughters to Mount St. Joseph Academy, a Catholic school in Rutland, according to the lawsuit. The private school doesn’t qualify for the state’s tuition program because it’s within a district that has a public high school, according to the lawsuit. 
The Bishops, in their lawsuit, are asking their school district to pay for one of their daughters, who is a senior in high school, to attend the Catholic school and to allow her participation in the state’s dual enrollment program, which offers high schoolers college courses free of cost. Students in private schools only qualify for dual enrollment if they receive public tuition. 
The complaint names Vermont Education Secretary Zoie Saunders, as well as the State Board of Education and the Barstow Unified Union School District, as defendants. 
“Religious families want to be treated equal. They sue. They get in, and then Vermont changes the law or does some sort of work around to exclude them again. And obviously, that’s unconstitutional,” Reed said.
